title: Philosophy: Logic, Knowledge, Mind and Ethics

notes.body:
Core definitions
- An argument is a set of premises offered in support of a conclusion.
- Deductive validity: it is impossible for all the premises to be true and the conclusion false. Validity depends on logical form, not on whether the premises are actually true.
- Soundness: the argument is valid and all its premises are true.
- Inductive strength: the premises make the conclusion probable without guaranteeing it. Abductive reasoning, or inference to the best explanation, picks the hypothesis that best explains the evidence.

Propositional logic
- Connectives: ¬ (not), ∧ (and), ∨ (inclusive or), → (material conditional), ↔ (biconditional).
- P → Q is false only when P is true and Q is false.
- Valid forms: modus ponens (P → Q, P ⊢ Q), modus tollens (P → Q, ¬Q ⊢ ¬P), disjunctive syllogism (P ∨ Q, ¬P ⊢ Q) and hypothetical syllogism (P → Q, Q → R ⊢ P → R).
- Invalid forms: affirming the consequent (P → Q, Q ⊢ P) and denying the antecedent (P → Q, ¬P ⊢ ¬Q).
- Equivalences: De Morgan's laws, ¬(P ∧ Q) ≡ ¬P ∨ ¬Q and ¬(P ∨ Q) ≡ ¬P ∧ ¬Q. Contraposition, P → Q ≡ ¬Q → ¬P.
- Truth tables test validity: an argument is valid if no row makes every premise true and the conclusion false.

Predicate logic
- Quantifiers: ∀x (for all x) and ∃x (there is at least one x). 'All Fs are G' is ∀x(Fx → Gx). 'Some F is G' is ∃x(Fx ∧ Gx).
- Scope matters. ∀x∃y Loves(x, y), 'everyone loves someone', does not entail ∃y∀x Loves(x, y), 'someone is loved by everyone'.

Worked example
'If the Bank cuts rates, borrowing rises. Borrowing has risen. So the Bank cut rates.' This affirms the consequent. Take the row where P is false and Q is true: both premises are true and the conclusion is false, so the argument is invalid. Borrowing might have risen for another reason.

Paradoxes and limits
- The paradoxes of material implication: a false antecedent makes any conditional true. This suggests → does not capture ordinary 'if'.
- The sorites paradox, which arises from vague predicates.
- Gödel's first incompleteness theorem (1931): any consistent, effectively axiomatised formal system strong enough to express basic arithmetic contains true statements of arithmetic that it cannot prove.

Common pitfalls
- Calling a single statement 'valid', or an argument 'true'.
- Thinking a valid argument must have a true conclusion. Validity guarantees only that true premises lead to a true conclusion.
- Treating 'or' as exclusive.
- Misplacing quantifiers. 'All Fs are G' is not ∀x(Fx ∧ Gx).

The tripartite analysis
On the traditional account, S knows that p if and only if (i) p is true, (ii) S believes that p, and (iii) S is justified in believing that p. Plato's Theaetetus discusses a version.

Gettier cases (1963)
Gettier gave cases where someone has a justified true belief but seems not to know. Smith has strong evidence that Jones will get the job and that Jones has ten coins in his pocket. He infers that the man who will get the job has ten coins in his pocket. In fact Smith gets the job and, unknown to him, also has ten coins in his pocket. His belief is justified and true, but true only by luck.

Responses
- No false lemmas: add a fourth condition that the belief is not inferred from any falsehood. Barn-façade cases (Goldman 1976) seem to defeat this: the belief is non-inferential but still lucky.
- Reliabilism: a belief is justified if it is produced by a reliable process.
- Tracking or sensitivity (Nozick 1981): if p were false, S would not believe p.
- Safety (Sosa, Williamson): S could not easily have believed p falsely.
- Knowledge-first (Williamson 2000): knowledge cannot be analysed and is more basic than belief.
Zagzebski (1994) argues that any analysis which lets justification fall short of guaranteeing truth will face Gettier cases.

Internalism and externalism
Internalists hold that what justifies a belief must be accessible to the subject on reflection. Externalists, such as reliabilists, allow factors the subject cannot access. The new evil demon problem presses externalism: a deceived victim with experiences like ours seems equally justified.

The structure of justification
The regress argument pushes towards foundationalism (basic beliefs support the rest), coherentism (beliefs support each other) or infinitism (an unending chain of reasons).

Scepticism and responses
- Radical scepticism (the brain in a vat): (1) I don't know I'm not a BIV. (2) If I know I have hands, I know I'm not a BIV. (3) So I don't know I have hands.
- Moore ('Proof of an External World', 1939; 'Four Forms of Scepticism', 1959) insists he knows he has hands. The Moorean response runs the sceptical argument in reverse: I know I have hands, so I know I'm not a BIV.
- Denying closure (Dretske, Nozick) rejects premise 2.
- Contextualism (DeRose, Lewis) says the standards for 'know' vary with the conversational context.
- Putnam (1981) argues that 'I am a brain in a vat' is self-refuting on semantic externalism.

Common pitfalls
- Assuming Gettier cases show belief is not required for knowledge. They show that justified true belief is not sufficient.
- Confusing reliabilism with internalism.
- Reading Moore's argument as question-begging without explaining why.

Descartes: Meditations on First Philosophy (1641)
- Method of doubt. Descartes doubts the senses (they sometimes deceive), then everything sensory (the dream argument), then even mathematics (an evil demon could deceive him).
- The cogito. While he doubts, he must exist: 'I am, I exist' is true whenever he thinks it. The well-known formula 'cogito ergo sum' comes from the Discourse (1637) and the Principles.
- Clear and distinct perception as the criterion of truth. Its reliability depends on God's existence, which he argues for with the trademark argument (Meditation III) and the ontological argument (Meditation V).
- The Cartesian circle (raised by Arnauld): Descartes seems to use clear and distinct perception to prove God, and God to validate clear and distinct perception.
- Substance dualism: mind is thinking, unextended substance; body is extended substance.

Locke: An Essay Concerning Human Understanding (1689)
- Rejects innate ideas. Supposedly universal principles are not known by children or 'idiots' (Locke's term).
- The mind starts as 'white paper'. All ideas come from sensation and reflection, and divide into simple and complex.
- Primary qualities (solidity, extension, figure, motion, number) resemble our ideas of them. Secondary qualities (colour, taste, sound) are powers in objects to produce ideas that do not resemble them.
- Substance is 'something, I know not what' that supports qualities.
- Personal identity consists in continuity of consciousness, which memory extends backwards. The prince and the cobbler thought experiment illustrates it.
- Representative realism, which Berkeley pressed towards idealism.

Hume: Treatise (1739–40) and Enquiry (1748)
- Impressions are vivid and ideas are faint copies. The copy principle says every simple idea derives from an impression, and Hume uses it to test terms for meaning.
- Hume's fork: relations of ideas (demonstrable, a priori) versus matters of fact (known through experience).
- Causation: we never perceive a necessary connection, only constant conjunction. The idea of necessity comes from a habit of the mind.
- The problem of induction: inferring the unobserved from the observed assumes nature is uniform. That assumption cannot be shown a priori, and showing it from experience would be circular.
- The bundle theory of the self: introspection finds only perceptions, never a self.
- Is–ought: moral conclusions cannot be derived from purely factual premises without explanation.

Illustration
Russell's chicken expects food every morning, until the day its neck is wrung. Repetition strengthens expectation without justifying it.

Common pitfalls
- Saying Locke is an idealist.
- Treating Hume's problem as merely that induction is not deductively valid. His point is that it cannot be justified without circularity.
- Treating the cogito as a syllogism with a hidden premise ('whatever thinks exists'). Descartes denied this reading.

notes.h: Philosophy of mind: the mind–body problem
notes.body:
Substance dualism
- Descartes' conceivability argument: I can clearly and distinctly conceive my mind existing without my body. Whatever God can make separate can exist separately. So mind and body are distinct.
- Divisibility: bodies have parts, the mind has none.
- The interaction problem: Princess Elisabeth of Bohemia asked in 1643 how an unextended mind could move an extended body. Causal closure of the physical adds to the pressure.
- Property dualism: there is one substance, but mental properties are not physical properties.

Behaviourism
Logical behaviourism (Ryle, The Concept of Mind, 1949; Hempel) analyses mental terms as dispositions to behave. Ryle called dualism the 'dogma of the Ghost in the Machine' and a category mistake. Objections:
- Analyses are circular, since a belief produces behaviour only given desires.
- The super-Spartan (Putnam), who feels pain but never shows it.
- The asymmetry between first-person and third-person knowledge of mental states.

Mind–brain identity theory (Place 1956, Smart 1959)
Mental states are brain states, as a matter of empirical discovery, in the way lightning is electrical discharge. The objection from multiple realisability (Putnam 1967): pain could be realised in octopuses, silicon systems or aliens with different physiology.

Functionalism
Mental states are defined by their causal role: their typical causes (inputs), effects (outputs) and relations to other mental states. Objections:
- The Chinese room (Searle 1980): manipulating symbols is not understanding.
- Block's China brain (1978).
- Inverted qualia, and absent qualia.

Consciousness and qualia
- Nagel, 'What Is It Like to Be a Bat?' (1974): subjective character escapes objective description.
- Jackson's knowledge argument (1982): Mary, a scientist raised in a black-and-white room, knows all the physical facts about colour but learns something new when she first sees red. Replies include the ability hypothesis (Lewis, Nemirow) and the claim that she gains a new concept of an old fact.
- Chalmers' zombie argument (1996): beings physically identical to us but lacking consciousness are conceivable, so possible, so physicalism is false. Replies deny that conceivability entails possibility.

Other views
- Eliminative materialism (Churchland 1981): folk psychology is a false theory.
- Mental causation and exclusion (Kim). If physical effects already have sufficient physical causes, non-reductive mental properties seem epiphenomenal.

Worked example
Is Mary's argument valid? (1) Before her release Mary knows all the physical facts. (2) On release she learns a new fact. (3) So not all facts are physical. The argument is valid in form, so the debate is over whether its premises are true. It trades on 'learns a new fact'. The ability reply says she gains know-how, not a fact, which blocks premise 2.

Common pitfalls
- Confusing type identity with token identity.
- Thinking functionalism is a form of behaviourism. It allows internal states.
- Assuming that conceivability entails possibility without argument.

The problem
Determinism holds that the past together with the laws of nature fixes a unique future. If so, is anyone free or responsible? Indeterminism, true randomness, does not obviously help, because chance does not seem to be control.

Positions
- Hard determinism: determinism is true and incompatible with free will, so no one is free.
- Libertarianism: free will is incompatible with determinism, determinism is false, and we are free. Versions include agent causation (Reid; Chisholm 1964) and event-causal accounts (Kane 1996, with 'self-forming actions').
- Compatibilism: free will is compatible with determinism.
- Hard incompatibilism (Pereboom 2001): the free will needed for basic-desert responsibility is incompatible with determinism and is not supplied by event-causal indeterminism either. Agent causation is coherent but not credible, so we probably lack such free will.

Classical compatibilism
Hobbes and Hume ('liberty of spontaneity'): freedom is acting as one wills without external constraint. Hume's Enquiry (1748, §8) presents the dispute as largely verbal.

The consequence argument (van Inwagen 1983)
- If determinism is true, our acts follow from the laws of nature and events in the remote past.
- We have no power over the past or the laws.
- So we have no power over the consequences of these, including our present acts.
The argument depends on a transfer principle: powerlessness is passed on through entailment.

Frankfurt's contributions
- Frankfurt cases (1969) challenge the principle of alternate possibilities (PAP), which says one is responsible only if one could have done otherwise. In the case, Black would intervene to make Jones act if Jones were about to choose otherwise, but Jones chooses on his own. Jones seems responsible though he could not have done otherwise.
- The hierarchical account (1971): a free will is one where first-order desires conform to second-order volitions. The 'willing addict' and the 'unwilling addict' illustrate the difference.

Other accounts
- Reasons-responsiveness: Fischer and Ravizza (1998) on guidance control.
- Strawson, 'Freedom and Resentment' (1962): reactive attitudes such as resentment and gratitude are part of human life, and no metaphysical theory could justify giving them up.

Empirical challenge
Libet (1983) found a readiness potential before subjects reported deciding. Critics dispute the timing method and whether the readiness potential reflects a decision at all (Schurger et al. 2012).

Worked example
Does a Frankfurt case refute PAP? Defenders reply with the 'flicker of freedom'. Jones could still have shown the prior sign that triggers Black's intervention. Or the dilemma defence: if determinism holds, Black's predictor begs the question; if it doesn't, Jones keeps alternatives.

Common pitfalls
- Equating determinism with fatalism, the view that outcomes happen whatever we do.
- Assuming indeterminism secures freedom.
- Treating compatibilism as the claim that determinism is true. It is only the claim that freedom and determinism are compatible.

Consequentialism
The right act is the one that produces the best consequences.
- Classical utilitarianism. Bentham (1789) offered the felicific calculus. Mill's Utilitarianism (1861) distinguished higher and lower pleasures: competent judges who have experienced both prefer the higher.
- Act utilitarianism assesses each act by its consequences. Rule utilitarianism assesses acts by whether they follow rules whose general acceptance maximises utility.
- Preference utilitarianism (Hare, Singer).
- Objections:
  - Demandingness. Singer (1972) argued that we should prevent serious suffering when we can do so without sacrificing anything morally comparable, which makes heavy demands.
  - Justice and rights: punishing an innocent person to prevent a riot.
  - Integrity (Williams 1973): the cases of George the chemist and Jim and the Indians.
  - Separateness of persons (Rawls 1971).
  - Rule worship or collapse (Smart): if rule utilitarianism insists on a rule even when breaking it would do more good, that looks like irrational 'rule worship'; if it allows exceptions, it seems to collapse into act utilitarianism.

Deontology
Some acts are required or forbidden regardless of their consequences.
- Kant's categorical imperative. See the Kant note.
- Ross (1930): prima facie duties such as fidelity, reparation, gratitude, non-maleficence, beneficence, justice and self-improvement. When they conflict, judgement decides.
- The doctrine of double effect: harm foreseen as a side effect may be permissible where intending it would not be.
- Constraints against harming versus doing and allowing.
- Objections: rigidity (lying to a murderer at the door); the paradox of deontology (why not violate one constraint to prevent five violations?); and how to resolve conflicts between duties.

Virtue ethics
- Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics: eudaimonia (flourishing) is the human good. Virtues are stable character traits, each a mean between excess and deficiency; courage lies between rashness and cowardice. Practical wisdom (phronesis) is required.
- Modern revival: Anscombe, 'Modern Moral Philosophy' (1958); Foot; MacIntyre, After Virtue (1981); Hursthouse (1999). Hursthouse holds that an action is right if it is what a virtuous agent would characteristically do in the circumstances.
- Objections: it gives little action guidance; circularity; cultural relativity of virtues; situationist evidence against stable character traits (Doris; Harman).

Applied test case: the trolley problem
Foot (1967) introduced the problem, and Thomson developed it, including the 'footbridge' variant. Most people would divert the trolley to kill one rather than five, but would not push a large man off a footbridge to stop it. Act utilitarianism treats the two cases alike. Double effect and Kant's means principle distinguish them.

Common pitfalls
- Saying Mill simply counts pleasures as Bentham did, ignoring the qualitative distinction.
- Reducing deontology to 'following rules'.
- Claiming virtue ethics gives no guidance at all. Hursthouse's 'v-rules', such as 'do what is honest', provide some.

Metaethics asks what moral claims mean, whether they can be true, and how, if at all, we know them.

Cognitivism and non-cognitivism
- Cognitivism: moral judgements express beliefs that can be true or false.
- Non-cognitivism: they express non-cognitive states such as attitudes or plans.

Moral realism
Moral facts exist and do not depend on anyone's attitudes.
- Naturalist realism (the Cornell realists, such as Boyd and Brink): moral properties are natural properties, discovered a posteriori.
- Non-naturalism (Moore, Principia Ethica, 1903): goodness is a simple, indefinable, non-natural property known by intuition.
- Moore's open question argument: for any natural property N, 'This is N, but is it good?' remains an open question, so good is not N. Reply: it is a semantic test that ignores a posteriori identities such as water = H₂O.
- Hume's is–ought gap.

Anti-realism and error theory
- Mackie's error theory (Ethics: Inventing Right and Wrong, 1977): moral claims aim at objective truth but are all false. The argument from relativity: moral disagreement is best explained by different ways of life. The argument from queerness: objective values would be metaphysically and epistemically strange, because they would have to be intrinsically action-guiding.

Non-cognitivism
- Emotivism. Ayer (Language, Truth and Logic, 1936): 'stealing is wrong' expresses disapproval and is neither true nor false. Stevenson added the persuasive role of moral language.
- Prescriptivism (Hare): moral judgements are universalisable prescriptions.
- Quasi-realism (Blackburn): expressivists can earn the right to talk of moral truth.
- The Frege–Geach problem: 'lying is wrong' must mean the same in 'If lying is wrong, then getting your brother to lie is wrong' as when asserted alone. Yet in the conditional no attitude is expressed. Expressivism struggles to explain why modus ponens with moral premises is valid.

Other positions
- Relativism: moral truth is relative to cultures. It struggles to make sense of moral progress and reformers.
- Divine command theory faces the Euthyphro dilemma: is something good because God commands it, or commanded because good?

Motivation
- Motivational internalism: sincerely judging that one ought to do something entails some motivation to do it. Combined with the Humean theory of motivation (beliefs alone do not motivate), this supports non-cognitivism.
- The amoralist objection (Brink): someone who sincerely judges something wrong but is unmoved.

Worked example
Disagreement about eating meat persists among informed people. Mackie takes this as evidence against objective values. Realists reply that scientific disagreement does not show there are no scientific facts, and that much moral disagreement rests on non-moral facts.

Common pitfalls
- Confusing emotivism with subjectivism. 'I disapprove' reports a feeling and can be true; 'Boo!' expresses one and is neither true nor false.
- Collapsing metaethics into normative ethics.

Critique of Pure Reason (1781/1787)
- Distinctions: a priori/a posteriori (how something is known) and analytic/synthetic (whether the predicate is contained in the subject concept). Kant's key question is how synthetic a priori judgements are possible. His examples include '7 + 5 = 12', geometry, and 'every event has a cause'.
- The Copernican revolution: suppose objects conform to our cognition, rather than the reverse.
- Transcendental idealism. Space and time are forms of intuition (the Transcendental Aesthetic). We know appearances (phenomena), not things in themselves (noumena).
- 'Thoughts without content are empty, intuitions without concepts are blind.' The categories, such as causality and substance, are pure concepts of the understanding. The Transcendental Deduction argues that they apply necessarily to experience.
- Against Hume, causality is a condition of objective experience (the Second Analogy), not mere habit.
- The Transcendental Dialectic: reason overreaches into antinomies and claims about the soul and God.

Groundwork of the Metaphysics of Morals (1785)
- Only a good will is good without qualification.
- Moral worth requires acting from duty, not merely in accordance with it. The shopkeeper who gives correct change only for profit acts rightly but without moral worth.
- Hypothetical imperatives depend on desires. The categorical imperative binds unconditionally.
- Formula of Universal Law: act only on a maxim you can at the same time will to become a universal law. A contradiction in conception (the lying promise: universal false promising would destroy the practice of promising) yields a perfect duty. A contradiction in the will (refusing ever to help others) yields an imperfect duty.
- Formula of Humanity: treat humanity, in yourself and others, always as an end and never merely as a means.
- Formulas of Autonomy and the Kingdom of Ends: rational beings give the moral law to themselves.

Objections
- Emptiness (Hegel), and false positives and negatives in the universalisability test.
- Rigorism: the murderer at the door ('On a Supposed Right to Lie', 1797).
- The place of emotion (Williams's 'one thought too many').

Worked example
Maxim: 'When short of money, I will borrow and promise to repay, knowing I cannot.' If universalised, promises would no longer be believed, so the maxim could not even work. This is a contradiction in conception, and so a perfect duty not to make false promises. The Formula of Humanity agrees: the lender is used merely as a means.

Common pitfalls
- Reading the Universal Law test as consequentialist ('what if everyone did it?'). The contradiction is logical or practical, not a matter of bad outcomes.
- Dropping 'merely' from the Formula of Humanity. Using a cashier as a means is fine.
- Equating transcendental idealism with Berkeley's idealism.

cards.b: An argument is valid if and only if it is impossible for all its premises to be true while its conclusion is false. Validity is a matter of form, not actual truth.
An argument is sound if it is valid and all of its premises are true. A sound argument therefore has a true conclusion.
From P → Q and ¬Q, infer ¬P. It is a valid form.

cards.f: What is affirming the consequent? Is it valid?
cards.b: From P → Q and Q, inferring P. It is invalid: when P is false and Q is true, both premises are true and the conclusion false.

cards.f: When is a material conditional P → Q false?
cards.b: Only when P is true and Q is false. In every other row of the truth table it is true.

cards.f: Formalise 'All philosophers are mortal' and 'Some philosopher is Welsh'.
cards.b: ∀x(Px → Mx) and ∃x(Px ∧ Wx). The universal takes →; the existential takes ∧.
No. 'Everyone loves someone' does not entail 'someone is loved by everyone'. The converse entailment does hold.

cards.f: What are the paradoxes of material implication?
cards.b: Because P → Q is true whenever P is false or Q is true, a false antecedent or true consequent makes any conditional true, e.g. 'If the moon is cheese, 2 + 2 = 4'. This suggests → diverges from ordinary 'if'.

cards.f: What is the contrapositive of P → Q, and is it equivalent?
cards.b: ¬Q → ¬P. It is logically equivalent to P → Q. The converse Q → P and the inverse ¬P → ¬Q are not.

cards.f: What is inference to the best explanation?
cards.b: Abductive reasoning: inferring the hypothesis that would, if true, best explain the evidence, judged by virtues such as simplicity, scope and fit.

A paradox of vague predicates: one grain is not a heap, and adding one grain never turns a non-heap into a heap. Apparently true premises then lead to the conclusion that no number of grains makes a heap.

cards.f: State the tripartite (JTB) analysis of knowledge.
cards.b: S knows that p if and only if p is true, S believes that p, and S is justified in believing that p.
That justified true belief is not sufficient for knowledge. He gave cases where a belief is justified and true only by luck, so it is intuitively not knowledge.

Henry, driving through a region full of fake barn façades, looks at the one real barn and believes 'that is a barn'. His belief is justified and true, but lucky, so it is arguably not knowledge, even though it is not inferred from a falsehood.

cards.f: What is the 'no false lemmas' response to Gettier?
cards.b: Add a fourth condition: the belief must not be inferred from any false belief. Barn-façade cases, which involve no inference, are a standard counterexample.
A belief is justified, or counts as knowledge, if it is produced by a reliable belief-forming process, one that tends to produce true beliefs. It is an externalist view.
If p were false, S would not believe that p. Combined with closure failure, it lets Nozick say we know we have hands while not knowing we are not brains in vats.

Internalism: what justifies a belief must be accessible to the subject on reflection. Externalism: justifiers can include factors outside the subject's awareness, such as the reliability of a process.

cards.f: Set out the brain-in-a-vat sceptical argument.
cards.b: (1) I don't know that I'm not a brain in a vat. (2) If I know I have hands, I know I'm not a brain in a vat. (3) So I don't know that I have hands.

cards.f: How does Moore respond to scepticism?
cards.b: He reverses the argument. He is more certain that he has hands than of any sceptical premise, so by modus ponens he knows that he is not being radically deceived.
The truth conditions of 'S knows that p' vary with the context of the speaker. In ordinary contexts we truly say we know we have hands; in sceptical contexts the standards rise and we do not.

cards.f: What is the principle of epistemic closure?
cards.b: If S knows p and knows that p entails q, then S knows (or is in a position to know) q. Sceptical arguments rely on it.
Knowledge is not analysable into belief plus other conditions. It is a basic mental state used to explain belief, evidence (E = K) and justification.
Foundationalism: some beliefs are basic and justify others, ending the regress. Coherentism: beliefs are justified by their mutual coherence within a system, with no privileged foundations.

cards.f: What are Descartes' three main stages of doubt in Meditation I?
cards.b: The senses sometimes deceive; the dream argument (I can't be sure I'm not dreaming); and the evil demon (a powerful deceiver could mislead me even about mathematics).
The objection (raised by Arnauld) that Descartes relies on clear and distinct perception to prove God exists, and then relies on God to guarantee clear and distinct perception.

Primary qualities (solidity, extension, figure, motion, number) exist in bodies and resemble our ideas of them. Secondary qualities (colour, taste, sound) are powers in objects to produce ideas that do not resemble anything in them.

cards.f: What is Locke's argument against innate ideas?
cards.b: There are no universally assented principles: children and 'idiots' lack them. Even if there were universal assent, it could be explained by experience, so innateness adds nothing.

cards.f: What is Locke's account of personal identity?
cards.b: A person is the same person as far as their consciousness extends backwards to past thoughts and actions, so memory continuity rather than sameness of substance constitutes personal identity.
All our simple ideas are copies of earlier impressions. Hume uses it as a test of meaning: if no impression gives rise to an idea, the term is suspect.
The division of objects of enquiry into relations of ideas, known a priori and necessary, and matters of fact, known only through experience and contingent.
Inferences from observed to unobserved cases assume nature is uniform. This cannot be shown a priori (its denial is conceivable), and arguing from past success would be circular.

cards.f: What is Hume's account of necessary connection?
cards.b: We never observe necessary connection between causes and effects, only constant conjunction. The idea of necessity arises from a felt determination of the mind to pass from one to the other.

cards.f: What is Hume's bundle theory of the self?
cards.b: On introspection Hume never finds a self, only particular perceptions. The self is 'nothing but a bundle or collection of different perceptions'.
I have an idea of an infinite, perfect God. The cause of an idea must have at least as much reality as the idea's content, and I am finite, so only God could have caused it.

cards.f: State Descartes' conceivability argument for dualism.
cards.b: I can clearly and distinctly conceive my mind existing without my body; whatever can be clearly and distinctly conceived apart can exist apart (God could make it so); therefore mind and body are distinct.
How can an unextended, non-physical mind cause changes in an extended, physical body, and vice versa? Princess Elisabeth pressed it on Descartes in 1643.
The view that statements about mental states can be translated into statements about behaviour and dispositions to behave (Ryle, Hempel).

cards.f: What is mind–brain type identity theory?
cards.b: Each type of mental state is identical with a type of brain state, an a posteriori identity like lightning = electrical discharge (Place 1956; Smart 1959).

cards.f: What is the multiple realisability objection?
cards.b: The same mental state, such as pain, could be realised by different physical states in different creatures (octopuses, aliens, robots), so it cannot be identical with any one brain-state type (Putnam 1967).
Mental states are defined by their causal role: their typical causes, effects on behaviour, and relations to other mental states, whatever physically realises them.
A person who follows rules for manipulating Chinese symbols can produce fluent answers without understanding Chinese. So running a program (syntax) is not sufficient for understanding (semantics).
Mary knows all the physical facts about colour vision but has never seen colour. On first seeing red she learns something new, so not all facts are physical.

cards.f: What is the ability hypothesis reply to Mary?
cards.b: Mary gains new abilities (to recognise, imagine and remember red), knowledge-how rather than knowledge of a new fact (Lewis, Nemirow).

Zombies, physical duplicates of us without consciousness, are conceivable. What is conceivable is possible. If zombies are possible, consciousness is not entailed by the physical, so physicalism is false.
Type identity: each kind of mental state is a kind of physical state. Token identity: each particular mental event is some physical event, allowing different physical types for the same mental type.
Folk psychology is a false theory; beliefs and desires as we conceive them do not exist and will be replaced by neuroscience (Churchland 1981).
The thesis that the state of the world at any time, together with the laws of nature, fixes a unique future.
Compatibilism: free will and moral responsibility are compatible with determinism. Incompatibilism: they are not, which leads either to libertarianism or to hard determinism.
Freedom as acting according to the determinations of the will, without external constraint, as opposed to a 'liberty of indifference' (uncaused choice), which Hume rejects.

If determinism is true, our acts are consequences of the laws of nature and the remote past. We have no power over the laws or the past, so we have no power over their consequences, including our acts.

cards.f: What is the principle of alternate possibilities (PAP)?
cards.b: A person is morally responsible for what they did only if they could have done otherwise.

cards.f: Describe a Frankfurt case and its purpose.
cards.b: Black will intervene to make Jones act if Jones shows any sign of choosing otherwise, but Jones chooses on his own, so Black never intervenes. Jones seems responsible though he could not have done otherwise, which challenges PAP.

cards.f: What is Frankfurt's hierarchical account of free will?
cards.b: A person acts freely when the first-order desire that moves them conforms to their second-order volition, a desire about which desire should be effective.

cards.f: What is the luck objection to libertarianism?
cards.b: If a choice is undetermined, then given the same past it could have gone either way, so which way it went seems a matter of chance rather than the agent's control.
The libertarian view that free actions are caused by the agent as a substance, not by prior events (Reid; Chisholm).

cards.f: What is the central idea of P. F. Strawson's 'Freedom and Resentment' (1962)?
cards.b: Moral responsibility is grounded in our reactive attitudes (resentment, gratitude, indignation). No metaphysical truth about determinism could rationally require us to abandon them.
Fatalism says what will happen will happen whatever we do. Determinism says what happens is fixed by prior causes, which include our deliberations and choices.

cards.f: State the principle of utility (classical utilitarianism).
cards.b: The right act is the one that produces the greatest total balance of happiness (pleasure over pain) for all affected.
Act: an act is right if it maximises utility. Rule: an act is right if it conforms to rules whose general acceptance would maximise utility.

cards.f: What is Mill's distinction between higher and lower pleasures?
cards.b: Pleasures differ in quality as well as quantity. Higher (intellectual, moral) pleasures are those that competent judges who know both decisively prefer.

Utilitarianism treats agents as channels for producing best outcomes, ignoring the moral significance of their own projects and commitments, as in his cases of George the chemist and Jim and the Indians.

cards.f: Name four of Ross's prima facie duties.
cards.b: Any four of: fidelity, reparation, gratitude, justice, beneficence, self-improvement, non-maleficence.

cards.f: State the doctrine of double effect.
cards.b: It may be permissible to bring about a harm as a foreseen side effect of pursuing a good end when it would be impermissible to intend that harm as a means or end, provided the good is proportionate.

cards.f: Distinguish the trolley case from the footbridge case.
cards.b: In the trolley case most people judge it permissible to divert a trolley so it kills one instead of five. In the footbridge case most judge it impermissible to push a man off a bridge to stop it, though the numbers are the same.
Flourishing or living well: the highest human good, consisting in activity of the soul in accordance with virtue over a complete life.

cards.f: What is Aristotle's doctrine of the mean?
cards.b: A virtue is a disposition to feel and act in the right way, at a mean between vices of excess and deficiency relative to us, e.g. courage between rashness and cowardice.
An action is right if and only if it is what a virtuous agent would characteristically do in the circumstances.

cards.f: What is the situationist challenge to virtue ethics?
cards.b: Social psychology suggests behaviour depends heavily on minor situational factors rather than stable character traits, questioning whether robust virtues exist (Doris; Harman).

cards.f: What does Singer argue in 'Famine, Affluence, and Morality' (1972)?
cards.b: If we can prevent something very bad without sacrificing anything of comparable moral importance, we ought to. Distance and the inaction of others make no moral difference, so affluent people should give far more.
Cognitivism: moral judgements express beliefs that are truth-apt. Non-cognitivism: they express non-cognitive attitudes (approval, plans, prescriptions) and are not straightforwardly true or false.
For any natural property N, 'X is N, but is X good?' is a meaningful open question. If good meant N, it would be closed. So good is not identical with any natural property.
The alleged mistake of identifying goodness with a natural property such as pleasure. Moore held that goodness is simple, indefinable and non-natural.

cards.f: What is Mackie's argument from queerness?
cards.b: Objective values would be entities unlike anything else, intrinsically action-guiding, and knowing them would need a special faculty. So it is more plausible there are none.
Moral judgements aim to state objective moral facts, but there are no such facts, so all positive moral judgements are false (Mackie 1977).
The non-cognitivist view that moral judgements express the speaker's emotions or attitudes and seek to influence others, e.g. 'Stealing is wrong' ≈ 'Stealing, boo!' (Ayer 1936; Stevenson).

Moral sentences keep their meaning in unasserted contexts such as conditionals, where no attitude is expressed. Expressivists must explain this and why arguments like modus ponens with moral premises are valid.
An expressivist programme seeking to explain how we can legitimately use realist-sounding talk of moral truth and facts while holding that moral judgements express attitudes.
Necessarily, if someone sincerely judges that they ought to do something, they are at least somewhat motivated to do it.
Is something good because God commands it, making goodness arbitrary? Or does God command it because it is good, making goodness independent of God's will?

Subjectivism: 'X is wrong' reports the speaker's disapproval, so it is true or false. Emotivism: it expresses disapproval and is neither, which avoids the problem that subjectivism makes moral disagreement impossible.
Analytic: the predicate is contained in the subject concept ('all bodies are extended'). Synthetic: the predicate adds something new ('all bodies are heavy').
Instead of assuming our cognition must conform to objects, Kant supposes objects must conform to our cognition, explaining how synthetic a priori knowledge of them is possible.
Space, time and the categories are forms our minds impose on experience. We know things as they appear (phenomena), not as they are in themselves (noumena).

cards.f: Give an example Kant counts as synthetic a priori.
cards.b: '7 + 5 = 12', geometrical truths, and 'every event has a cause'.

cards.f: State the Formula of Universal Law.
cards.b: Act only according to that maxim through which you can at the same time will that it become a universal law.
Act so that you treat humanity, whether in your own person or another's, always at the same time as an end and never merely as a means.

cards.f: Contradiction in conception vs contradiction in the will
cards.b: A contradiction in conception: the maxim cannot even be coherently universalised (lying promise), giving perfect duties. A contradiction in the will: it can be conceived but not consistently willed (never helping others), giving imperfect duties.
Hypothetical imperatives command conditionally on a desired end ('if you want X, do Y'). The categorical imperative commands unconditionally, independent of desires.
A shopkeeper who gives correct change because honesty is good for business acts in accordance with duty, but not from duty, so the act lacks moral worth.

cards.f: What does Kant say about lying to the murderer at the door?
cards.b: In 'On a Supposed Right to Lie' (1797) he holds that truthfulness is an unconditional duty, so even lying to save a friend from a murderer is wrong. Critics take this as evidence of rigorism.

cards.f: What is the 'empty formalism' objection to Kant?
cards.b: Hegel's objection: the universalisability test is purely formal, so by itself it cannot generate substantive duties. Whether a maxim yields a contradiction depends on content (such as the institution of property) brought in from outside. A related later objection is that the test gives false positives (some immoral maxims universalise consistently) and false negatives (some innocent ones apparently do not).

questions.q: Which of the following argument forms is INVALID?
questions.why: This is denying the antecedent. If P is false and Q is true, both premises hold but the conclusion fails. The others are modus ponens, modus tollens and disjunctive syllogism.

questions.q: Which formula correctly translates 'No student is idle' (Sx: x is a student; Ix: x is idle)?
questions.why: 'No S is I' says that anything which is a student is not idle. The first option wrongly says everything is a student. The last two say only that some student is not idle.

questions.q: What did Gettier's 1963 counterexamples aim to show?
options: Justified true belief is not sufficient for knowledge
Justification is not necessary for knowledge
We can never know anything about the external world
questions.why: Gettier's cases are justified true beliefs that seem not to be knowledge because they are true by luck. They attack the sufficiency of the tripartite analysis, not the necessity of its conditions.

questions.q: Which response to radical scepticism accepts that we know we have hands while denying that we know we are not brains in vats?
questions.why: Nozick's sensitivity account lets one know p (I have hands) without knowing q (I'm not a BIV), even though p entails q. That means giving up closure. Moore keeps closure and asserts both pieces of knowledge.

questions.q: According to Locke, which of the following is a secondary quality?
questions.why: For Locke, colour is a power in bodies to produce ideas in us that resemble nothing in the bodies themselves. Shape, motion and solidity are primary qualities.

questions.q: Hume argues that the principle that the future will resemble the past cannot be justified by experience because:
options: Any such argument would assume the very principle it tries to prove
The principle is a relation of ideas
We have no impressions of the past
questions.why: Arguing that induction has worked before and so will keep working relies on induction, so the justification is circular. The principle is not a relation of ideas, because its denial is conceivable.

questions.q: Which objection is most directly aimed at mind–brain type identity theory?
questions.why: If pain can be realised in physically different systems, it cannot be identical with one brain-state type (Putnam 1967). The Chinese room targets functionalism, the super-Spartan targets behaviourism, and Frege–Geach belongs to metaethics.

questions.q: Frankfurt-style cases are designed to challenge which principle?
options: The causal closure of the physical
The transfer principle in the consequence argument
questions.why: They describe agents who could not have done otherwise yet seem responsible. That counts against PAP, the claim that responsibility requires the ability to do otherwise.

questions.q: Which philosopher distinguished higher from lower pleasures?
questions.why: Mill, in Utilitarianism (1861), argued that pleasures differ in quality as well as quantity. Bentham measured pleasure only by quantitative dimensions such as intensity and duration.

questions.q: The Frege–Geach problem poses a difficulty principally for:
questions.why: Expressivists say moral sentences express attitudes, but in unasserted contexts such as 'if lying is wrong…' no attitude is expressed. They must then explain how the meaning stays the same and why moral modus ponens is valid.

questions.q: According to Kant, a maxim that generates a contradiction in conception when universalised indicates:
questions.why: If a maxim cannot even be conceived as universal law, like the lying promise, there is a perfect duty not to act on it. A contradiction in the will grounds imperfect duties.

questions.q: Using a truth table, show whether the following argument is valid: P → Q; Q → R; therefore P → R.
markScheme: Constructs a truth table covering all eight rows of P, Q, R
Correctly computes P → Q, Q → R and P → R in each row
Identifies that the only rows where P → R is false are those with P true and R false
Shows that in those rows at least one premise is false, so the argument (hypothetical syllogism) is valid
questions.modelAnswer: P → R is false only when P is true and R is false, which happens in two of the eight rows. If Q is true there, Q → R is false (T → F). If Q is false, P → Q is false (T → F). So no row has both premises true and the conclusion false, and the argument is valid. This is hypothetical syllogism.

questions.q: Explain the difference between a valid argument and a sound argument, with an example of a valid but unsound argument.
markScheme: Valid: impossible for the premises to be true and the conclusion false; sound: valid with true premises
Gives a correct example of a valid argument with at least one false premise
questions.modelAnswer: An argument is valid when its form guarantees that true premises would give a true conclusion. It is sound when it is valid and its premises really are true. 'All fish can fly; salmon are fish; so salmon can fly' is valid, because the conclusion follows. It is unsound because the first premise is false.

questions.q: Explain one Gettier-style counterexample to the tripartite analysis of knowledge, and identify which feature of the case makes it a counterexample.
markScheme: Describes a clear Gettier case (e.g. Smith and the ten coins, the stopped clock, or barn façades)
Shows the belief is true
Shows the belief is justified
Identifies epistemic luck: the justification is disconnected from what makes the belief true
questions.modelAnswer: Smith has strong evidence that Jones will get the job and that Jones has ten coins in his pocket. He infers that the man who will get the job has ten coins in his pocket. In fact Smith himself gets the job and, unknown to him, also has ten coins. His belief is true, and it is justified by good evidence and valid inference. Yet it seems not to be knowledge. What makes the belief true (Smith's own coins) is unconnected to his reasons (facts about Jones). It is true by luck.

questions.q: Outline Hume's account of the idea of causation, explaining how it relies on the copy principle.
markScheme: States the copy principle: all ideas derive from impressions
Identifies the components of the idea of cause: contiguity, priority and necessary connection
Observes that no impression of necessary connection is found in single instances of cause and effect
Explains that repeated observation of constant conjunction produces a habit or customary transition in the mind
Concludes that the idea of necessity is copied from this internal impression of determination, projected onto objects
questions.modelAnswer: Hume's copy principle says every simple idea copies an earlier impression, so to clarify 'cause' we look for its source. In a single case we observe only contiguity and priority: one billiard ball strikes, the other moves. We see no necessary connection. After repeatedly observing such pairs, constant conjunction, the mind is determined by habit to expect the second on seeing the first. That felt determination is an internal impression. The idea of necessary connection is copied from it and then mistakenly projected onto the objects themselves.

questions.q: Explain functionalism and one objection to it.
markScheme: Mental states are defined by their causal or functional role
Role includes relations to inputs, outputs and other mental states
Functionalism allows multiple realisability
Explains a relevant objection clearly (e.g. Chinese room, inverted or absent qualia, China brain)
questions.modelAnswer: Functionalism says a mental state is defined by what it does, not what it is made of. Pain is the state typically caused by bodily damage that causes distress, wincing and a desire to avoid the cause, and interacts with other mental states. Anything that plays that role, whether neurons, silicon or alien tissue, is in pain. Block's China brain is one objection. If the population of China, linked by radios, reproduced the functional organisation of a brain, functionalism implies the system would have mental states. Intuitively it would have no experiences, which suggests that functional role misses qualia.

questions.q: Explain the luck objection to libertarianism, and briefly assess one libertarian response.
markScheme: Libertarianism requires that free choices be undetermined
Objection: if the past and laws are compatible with either choice, the difference between them is a matter of chance, not control
Response: e.g. agent causation, or Kane's self-forming actions and dual efforts
Assessment: e.g. agent causation is obscure, or Kane's account may relocate rather than remove the luck
questions.modelAnswer: Libertarians hold that free choices are not determined. But if everything about Anna up to the moment of choice is compatible with her choosing either A or B, nothing about her explains why she chose A rather than B. The difference looks like luck. Kane replies that in self-forming actions the agent makes efforts towards both options. Whichever succeeds is endorsed as hers, so she is responsible either way. Critics answer that which effort succeeds is still undetermined, so the luck has moved rather than vanished.

questions.q: Distinguish act from rule utilitarianism, and explain why rule utilitarianism may 'collapse' into act utilitarianism.
markScheme: Act utilitarianism: an act is right if it maximises utility
Rule utilitarianism: an act is right if it follows rules whose general acceptance maximises utility
Collapse objection: if breaking a rule would produce more utility in a case, a utility-focused rule should allow an exception
Adding exceptions makes the rules match act utilitarian verdicts; refusing looks like 'rule worship' (Smart)
questions.modelAnswer: Act utilitarianism judges each act by whether it produces the best consequences. Rule utilitarianism judges acts by whether they follow rules whose general acceptance would maximise utility, such as 'do not punish the innocent'. The collapse objection asks what happens when breaking a rule would produce more good. If the rule utilitarian adds exceptions for such cases, the refined rules end up giving the same verdicts as act utilitarianism. If they insist on keeping the rule, they seem to value rule-following over the welfare that justified the rule, which Smart called 'rule worship'.

questions.q: Outline Mackie's argument from relativity, and give one realist reply.
markScheme: Notes the extensive variation in moral codes across societies and times
Mackie: this is better explained by people's participation in different ways of life than by differing perceptions of objective values
Supports error theory or anti-realism as the best explanation
Realist reply: e.g. disagreement exists in science too; many disagreements stem from differing non-moral beliefs or applications of shared principles
questions.modelAnswer: Moral codes vary widely between societies and periods. Mackie argues the best explanation is that moral views reflect people's adherence to and participation in different ways of life, not that some perceive objective values more accurately than others. Moral beliefs follow ways of life rather than the other way round, which supports his error theory. Realists reply that disagreement does not show there is nothing to be right about. Science has had long disagreements too. Much moral disagreement may come from different factual beliefs, such as beliefs about the afterlife, applied to shared principles.

questions.q: Apply Kant's Formula of Universal Law to the maxim 'When I am in need of money, I will borrow it and promise to repay, knowing I never will.'
markScheme: Formulates the maxim and imagines it as a universal law
If everyone made false promises when in need, promises would no longer be believed
The maxim would then be unable to achieve its purpose, a contradiction in conception
Concludes there is a perfect duty not to make lying promises
questions.modelAnswer: We imagine a world in which everyone in need of money makes promises they intend to break. In such a world no one would accept a promise of repayment, and the practice of promising would collapse. The maxim could not achieve its end, getting money through a promise, because it depends on the trust that universal false promising would destroy. It cannot even be conceived as a universal law without contradiction. So there is a perfect duty not to act on it.

questions.q: Explain what Kant means by a synthetic a priori judgement, and why such judgements are central to the Critique of Pure Reason.
markScheme: Synthetic: the predicate is not contained in the subject concept, so it extends knowledge
A priori: known independently of experience, with necessity and strict universality
Examples: mathematics, e.g. 7 + 5 = 12; 'every event has a cause'
Central question 'how are synthetic a priori judgements possible?', answered via the Copernican turn and transcendental idealism; this also responds to Hume
questions.modelAnswer: A synthetic judgement adds something not contained in its subject concept. An a priori judgement is known independently of experience, and is necessary and strictly universal. Kant holds that mathematics ('7 + 5 = 12') and the principles underlying natural science ('every event has a cause') are both synthetic and a priori. Hume's fork had no room for such knowledge. Kant's question is how it is possible. His answer is that space, time and the categories are conditions our cognition imposes on experience, so we can know a priori that objects of possible experience conform to them.

questions.q:
Consider the following argument from a student's essay:
'If God exists, there is no pointless suffering. If there is no pointless suffering, then every evil serves a greater good. But some evils, such as a fawn dying slowly in a forest fire, serve no greater good. So God does not exist.'
(a) Formalise the argument in propositional logic, using clearly stated letters. (b) Determine whether it is valid, showing your reasoning. (c) Assess whether it is sound, identifying which premise is most open to challenge and why.
markScheme: Assigns sentence letters correctly (e.g. G: God exists; N: there is no pointless suffering; E: every evil serves a greater good)
Premises: G → N; N → E; ¬E. Conclusion: ¬G
Shows validity: hypothetical syllogism gives G → E; modus tollens with ¬E gives ¬G
Or shows validity by truth table / reductio (assume G, derive E, contradict ¬E)
Distinguishes validity from soundness
Identifies the evidential premise (¬E) as most contested: we may be unable to see goods that justify evil (sceptical theism)
Considers challenges to G → N (e.g. free-will theodicy, natural law theodicy)
Notes that the N → E link is close to analytic given the definition of 'pointless'
Refers to the fawn example from Rowe (1979)
Reaches a clear evaluative judgement
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) Let G = 'God exists', N = 'there is no pointless suffering' and E = 'every evil serves a greater good'. The premises are G → N, N → E and ¬E. The conclusion is ¬G.

(b) The argument is valid. From G → N and N → E, hypothetical syllogism gives G → E. With ¬E, modus tollens gives ¬G. Equivalently, suppose G. Then N and E follow by modus ponens, contradicting ¬E, so ¬G. No assignment of truth values makes all three premises true and the conclusion false.

(c) Validity guarantees only that if the premises are true, the conclusion is true. Soundness needs true premises. The second premise is close to analytic. 'Pointless suffering' just means suffering that serves no greater good, so if none exists, every evil serves some good. The first premise has strong support from the traditional idea of God as omnipotent, omniscient and perfectly good. Such a being would, it seems, prevent any suffering not needed for a greater good. Theists may still question it with free-will or natural-law theodicies.

The weakest point is the factual premise ¬E, illustrated by the case of the fawn, which Rowe (1979) used. That we cannot see any good served by the fawn's suffering does not obviously show there is none. Sceptical theists argue that our grasp of possible goods is too limited for 'I see no reason' to imply 'there is no reason'. Rowe himself made the claim probabilistic: it is reasonable to believe some suffering is pointless, so the argument supports atheism inductively rather than proving it.

So the student's argument is formally valid, but its soundness depends on the contested evidential premise. It is better presented as an argument that makes atheism probable than as a deductive proof.

questions.q: Evaluate the claim that radical scepticism can be refuted by appeal to ordinary knowledge, as Moore attempted.
markScheme: Sets out the closure-based sceptical argument (BIV) clearly
Explains Moore's 'Proof of an External World' (1939): here is one hand… so external things exist; and the Moorean reversal
Explains why Moore claims greater certainty for 'I have hands' than for sceptical premises
Objection: question-begging / dialectical ineffectiveness against the sceptic
Distinguishes justification (warrant) from persuading the sceptic; transmission failure (Wright)
Considers dogmatism (Pryor) as a modern development
Compares alternative responses: denying closure (Nozick, Dretske) and its costs (abominable conjunctions)
Compares contextualism (DeRose, Lewis) as explaining the sceptic's appeal
Considers externalist responses (reliabilism) that support Moorean knowledge
Reaches a reasoned judgement
questions.modelAnswer:
The sceptic reasons: (1) I don't know that I'm not a brain in a vat. (2) If I know I have hands, I know I'm not a BIV, by closure. (3) So I don't know I have hands. Moore, in 'Proof of an External World' (1939), held up his hands and argued that since here is one hand and here is another, external things exist. More generally, he reversed the sceptic's modus tollens into a modus ponens. He is more certain that he has hands than of any premise in a sceptical argument, so he knows he is not radically deceived.

Moore has a real point. Arguments can only be as convincing as their premises, and ordinary perceptual knowledge seems more secure than abstract principles about vats. Pryor's dogmatism develops this. Perceptual experience gives immediate, defeasible justification without first needing evidence against sceptical hypotheses.

The standard objection is that Moore begs the question. The sceptic doubts precisely whether perception gives knowledge, so citing perceptual knowledge seems to assume what is disputed. Wright argues that warrant fails to transmit here. My experience supports 'I have hands' only if I am already entitled to assume I am not a BIV, so the inference cannot give me new reason to reject the sceptical hypothesis. The reply is that refuting scepticism might mean showing that we know, not convincing the sceptic. An externalist can hold that Moore's belief was reliably formed and so counts as knowledge, whether or not he can prove this from scratch.

The alternatives have costs. Denying closure (Nozick) allows 'abominable conjunctions' such as 'I know I have hands but don't know I'm not a handless BIV'. Contextualism explains why scepticism is tempting but says the sceptic is right in sceptical contexts.

Moore therefore shows that scepticism does not force us to give up ordinary knowledge claims, and with externalist support his position is defensible. But he does not refute scepticism in a way that would move someone who already doubts, so 'refuted' overstates what he achieved.

questions.q: 'The search for a fourth condition on knowledge is doomed: any analysis that allows justification without guaranteed truth will face Gettier cases.' Discuss.
markScheme: Sets out the tripartite analysis and Gettier's challenge with an example
Explains Zagzebski's (1994) argument: a recipe for generating Gettier cases from any fallible justification condition
Assesses no-false-lemmas and its counterexamples (barn façades)
Assesses defeasibility accounts and problems (misleading defeaters)
Assesses sensitivity (Nozick) and problems (closure failure, some counterexamples)
Assesses safety (Sosa, Williamson, Pritchard) as an anti-luck condition
Considers virtue epistemology (credit / success from ability) and fake-barn worries
Considers infallibilism as a way out and its sceptical cost
Considers knowledge-first epistemology (Williamson) as rejecting the project
Discusses whether failure of analysis matters (Wittgensteinian or family-resemblance views)
Uses examples to test each proposal
Reaches a well-argued conclusion
questions.modelAnswer:
Gettier showed that justified true belief can be true by luck, as when Smith's belief about the man with ten coins is made true by his own coins. Since then philosophers have looked for a fourth condition to exclude such luck.

Zagzebski (1994) argued that the search cannot succeed. Take any analysis where the justification or warrant condition does not entail truth. Start with a case where a justified belief is false. Then add a stroke of good luck that makes it true for unrelated reasons. The result meets every condition but is still lucky. The only escape is a condition that entails truth, and that seems to make the truth condition redundant or to lead to scepticism.

The main proposals bear her out. No-false-lemmas fails in barn-façade cases, where no inference is involved. Defeasibility analyses struggle with misleading defeaters, truths that would undermine justification only because they are misleading. Nozick's sensitivity condition handles some Gettier cases but gives up closure and misjudges others. Safety, the requirement that one could not easily have been wrong, does better. Yet determining which nearby worlds count can look tailored to the cases. Virtue theories, where true belief must be credited to the agent's competence, struggle with barn façades, since Henry's perceptual competence is working perfectly.

The thesis is not established, however. Zagzebski's recipe assumes the fourth condition is independent of truth. Safety and some virtue conditions are factive or modal in a way that resists her construction: a belief that is true only by luck is precisely one that is not safe. Infallibilism would avoid Gettier cases but at the price of scepticism about ordinary knowledge.

The deepest response is Williamson's (2000). The failure of decades of analysis shows that knowledge is basic. It is not belief plus extra conditions, and it can explain justification and evidence rather than being explained by them.

Overall, Zagzebski's argument shows that analyses built from independent, fallible components are doomed. It does not show that every attempt to say what knowledge is must fail. Knowledge may resist conceptual analysis without being mysterious.

questions.q: Explain and evaluate Descartes' argument in the Meditations that he can be certain he exists.
markScheme: Explains the method of doubt and its purpose (finding an indubitable foundation)
Explains the stages of doubt: senses, dreaming, evil demon
States the cogito as in Meditation II: 'I am, I exist' is necessarily true whenever conceived
Notes its performative or self-verifying character (whenever I think it, it must be true)
Discusses whether it is an inference with a hidden premise ('whatever thinks exists') and Descartes' replies
Objection (Lichtenberg, Russell): Descartes is only entitled to 'there is thinking', not to a substantial 'I'
Objection: Hume's bundle theory, since introspection reveals no persisting self
Discusses what 'I' can be known to be at this point (a thinking thing) and whether this supports dualism
Considers that the cogito's certainty may hold only in the present moment
Reaches a reasoned conclusion
questions.modelAnswer:
In the Meditations Descartes seeks a foundation for knowledge that resists all doubt. He doubts the senses because they sometimes deceive. He doubts all sensory belief because he cannot rule out dreaming. Then he doubts even mathematics, since an all-powerful deceiver might mislead him about it. In Meditation II he finds something the deceiver cannot touch. If he is deceived, he must exist to be deceived. So 'I am, I exist' is necessarily true whenever he puts it forward or conceives it.

The argument's strength is that it verifies itself. Doubting one's existence is a form of thinking, so it confirms what it doubts. Descartes denied in the Second Replies that it is a syllogism relying on the general premise 'everything that thinks exists'. He claimed it is grasped by a simple intuition of the mind. That matters, because a general premise would itself be open to doubt by the demon.

The strongest objection concerns the 'I'. Lichtenberg, and later Russell, argued that Descartes is entitled only to 'there is thinking' or 'thoughts are occurring'. Inferring a thinker, a substance that persists through time and owns these thoughts, assumes the grammar of subject and predicate. Hume reported that introspection reveals only perceptions, never a self, which supports the worry. Descartes might reply that thought is necessarily someone's thought. Whether that is a conceptual truth or a substantive metaphysical assumption is exactly what is disputed.

The certainty is also narrow. It holds only for the present moment, 'whenever I think it', and it says nothing about what I am beyond a thing that thinks. Descartes' move from this to dualism in Meditation VI needs further and much more contestable premises.

Descartes therefore establishes something indubitable: thinking is occurring, and in some minimal sense there is a subject of it. The cogito does not by itself secure a substantial, persisting, immaterial self.

questions.q: 'Locke's empiricism is undermined by his own account of substance.' Discuss with reference to Locke and at least one of Berkeley or Hume.
markScheme: Explains Locke's empiricism: all ideas from sensation and reflection; rejection of innate ideas
Explains Locke's account of substance as an unknown substratum, 'something, I know not what'
Identifies the tension: how can an empiricist have an idea of something never experienced?
Notes Locke's concession that our idea of substance is obscure and relative
Explains the primary/secondary quality distinction and representative realism
Berkeley's critique: material substratum is unintelligible; ideas can only resemble ideas; esse est percipi
Hume's critique: no impression of substance, so the idea is merely a collection of simple ideas; extended to the self
Considers defences of Locke (e.g. substance as a theoretical posit; nominal vs real essence)
Evaluates whether the tension is fatal or reveals a defensible modesty
Reaches a reasoned conclusion
questions.modelAnswer:
Locke argues that the mind begins as 'white paper' and that all ideas derive from sensation or reflection. Yet he also holds that qualities must inhere in some substance, a support he describes as 'something, I know not what'. The question is whether an empiricist can coherently believe in something of which no experience could give an idea.

Locke sees the problem. He admits that our idea of pure substance is obscure and only relative: we conceive it as whatever supports qualities, without any positive content. He reaches it by reasoning from the observation that qualities appear together and that we cannot conceive of them existing by themselves. Combined with his representative realism, in which primary qualities in bodies resemble our ideas while secondary qualities are mere powers, this yields a picture of a material world behind our ideas.

Berkeley argued that this picture collapses. An idea can resemble nothing but another idea, so the claim that ideas resemble material qualities is unintelligible. The distinction between primary and secondary qualities fails, because the variation Locke uses to show colours are mind-dependent applies equally to shape and size. A substratum of which nothing can be said is not a coherent idea at all. Consistent empiricism, Berkeley concluded, leads to idealism: to be is to be perceived.

Hume took the empiricist test further. Using the copy principle, he asked from which impression the idea of substance is derived and found none. The idea is only a collection of simple ideas joined by the imagination and given a name. He applied the same reasoning to the self.

Locke can be defended in part. His substratum resembles a theoretical posit, inferred to explain the observed grouping of qualities. His distinction between nominal and real essence shows an intended modesty about the limits of knowledge. But his own principles allow ideas only from experience, so a posit lacking any positive idea fits uneasily.

The tension is therefore real. It does not destroy empiricism, but it shows that Locke's version is unstable, as the developments by Berkeley and Hume suggest.

questions.q: Mary is a brilliant neuroscientist who has lived her whole life in a black-and-white room. Through books and black-and-white monitors she has learned every physical fact about colour vision: the wavelengths, retinal responses and neural processes involved. One day she leaves the room and sees a ripe tomato for the first time. Her colleague Dev says: 'Mary learns nothing new; she merely acquires new abilities.' Her other colleague, Sofia, insists: 'Mary learns a new fact, so physicalism is false.' Assess who is right.
markScheme: Sets out Jackson's (1982) knowledge argument in premise–conclusion form
Explains the significance for physicalism (completeness of physical facts)
Explains Dev's view: the ability hypothesis (Lewis, Nemirow): know-how, not knowledge-that
Evaluates the ability hypothesis, e.g. Mary seems to gain propositional knowledge ('so that is what red is like'), as embedded in conditionals
Explains the phenomenal concept strategy: new concept, old fact
Evaluates whether new concepts pick out non-physical properties
Considers the acquaintance reply (Conee)
Considers Dennett's denial that Mary would be surprised
Notes Jackson's own later rejection of the argument
Reaches a reasoned verdict on Dev vs Sofia
questions.modelAnswer:
Sofia is restating Jackson's (1982) knowledge argument. (1) Before release Mary knows every physical fact about colour vision. (2) On release she learns a new fact, what it is like to see red. (3) So not all facts are physical, and physicalism, the view that the physical facts are all the facts, is false.

Dev gives the ability hypothesis of Lewis and Nemirow. Mary gains knowledge-how: the ability to recognise, imagine and remember red. She does not gain knowledge that some new fact obtains. Abilities are not facts, so premise (2) is false. This captures something real, since Mary certainly gains these abilities. But it struggles with how her knowledge behaves. She can now think 'if seeing red is like this, then…' and reason with it, and propositional knowledge can be embedded in conditionals in this way. Mere abilities apparently cannot. Her exclamation 'so that's what red looks like!' seems to express knowledge that something is the case.

A stronger physicalist reply is the phenomenal concept strategy. Mary does learn something propositional, but she learns an old fact in a new way. On seeing red she acquires a phenomenal concept that picks out a physical property she already knew under a physical description, just as one might learn that Hesperus is Phosphorus. The knowledge is new while the fact is not. The worry is whether phenomenal concepts can be explained physically or whether they bring back what is distinctive about consciousness. Conee's acquaintance reply offers a third option: Mary becomes directly acquainted with a property, which is neither know-how nor a new fact. Dennett denies that Mary would be surprised at all, though this seems to beg the question.

Jackson himself later abandoned the argument and accepted physicalism.

Verdict: Sofia's conclusion does not follow, because premise (2) is ambiguous between a new fact and new knowledge of an old fact. But Dev's diagnosis is incomplete. The best physicalist answer is that Mary gains new propositional knowledge without learning a new fact.

questions.q: 'The conceivability of zombies shows that consciousness is not physical.' Discuss.
markScheme: Sets out the zombie argument (Chalmers 1996) in clear premises
Explains physicalism as supervenience / necessitation of the mental by the physical
Explains the link from conceivability to possibility and its pedigree in Descartes
Distinguishes prima facie from ideal conceivability; positive vs negative conceivability
Objection: zombies are not genuinely conceivable (e.g. Dennett)
Objection: a posteriori necessity (water = H₂O) shows conceivability may not entail possibility
Chalmers' two-dimensional reply: no gap between appearance and reality for consciousness
Phenomenal concept strategy explains the conceivability without non-physical properties
Considers type-B physicalism and the explanatory gap (Levine)
Considers the implication of epiphenomenalism if zombies are possible, and the self-stultification worry
Considers alternative conclusions (property dualism, Russellian monism)
Reaches a well-argued conclusion
questions.modelAnswer:
Chalmers' zombie argument runs as follows. (1) It is conceivable that there be a being physically identical to me but with no conscious experience, a zombie. (2) If zombies are conceivable, they are metaphysically possible. (3) If zombies are possible, the physical facts do not necessitate the facts about consciousness. (4) Physicalism requires that they do. So physicalism is false.

Some physicalists reject premise (1). Dennett argues that once we properly imagine a being with every functional and physical capacity of a conscious person, including discriminations and self-reports, nothing is left to remove. We only think we are imagining a zombie. Chalmers replies that what is needed is ideal, positive conceivability, and that consciousness seems clearly separable from structure and function.

The main battle concerns premise (2). Water = H₂O is necessary, yet it once seemed conceivable that water was not H₂O, so conceivability is a fallible guide to possibility. Chalmers' two-dimensional reply is that in the water case the illusion arises because 'water' picks out its referent by superficial features. Consciousness has no such gap, since how it seems is how it is. So the analogy fails.

Type-B physicalists accept that the explanatory gap (Levine) is real but deny that it reflects an ontological gap. The phenomenal concept strategy explains why: phenomenal concepts are conceptually isolated from physical concepts, so their connection cannot be grasped a priori even if they refer to physical properties. This accounts for the conceivability of zombies without non-physical properties. Its weakness is that phenomenal concepts must themselves be explained physically.

The conclusion also brings costs. If zombies are possible and the physical world is causally closed, consciousness seems epiphenomenal, and then our judgements about consciousness would be the same whether or not we were conscious. Russellian monism, which takes consciousness to be the intrinsic nature of physical structure, offers a middle way.

Overall, the argument shows that consciousness is not conceptually reducible to the physical. Whether it shows consciousness is non-physical depends on the disputed move from conceivability to possibility, so it falls short of a proof.

questions.q: Dr Ellis is a neurosurgeon who has secretly implanted a device in her patient Sam's brain. If Sam shows any sign of deciding not to vote for the Green candidate, the device will activate and cause him to vote Green. In fact, Sam decides on his own, for his own reasons, to vote Green, and the device never activates. Is Sam morally responsible for his vote? Use the case to assess the principle of alternate possibilities.
markScheme: Identifies the case as a Frankfurt-style case (Frankfurt 1969)
States PAP: responsible only if one could have done otherwise
Explains that Sam could not have done otherwise yet seems responsible because the device played no role
Concludes that, if the intuition holds, PAP is false and responsibility depends on actual sequence
Flicker of freedom reply: Sam could have shown the prior sign, a residual alternative
Reply to flicker: such flickers are too thin to ground responsibility
Dilemma defence (Kane, Widerker): if the prior sign determines the decision, the case assumes determinism; if not, Sam retains alternatives
Discusses refined Frankfurt cases (e.g. Mele and Robb) designed to avoid the dilemma
Relates to compatibilism and to accounts such as Fischer and Ravizza's guidance control
Reaches a reasoned verdict
questions.modelAnswer:
This is a Frankfurt-style case (Frankfurt 1969). It targets the principle of alternate possibilities (PAP): a person is morally responsible for what they did only if they could have done otherwise. Sam could not have done otherwise, because any move towards another choice would have triggered the device. Yet the device never acted. Sam reasoned and chose exactly as he would have without it. Intuitively, he is as responsible as anyone who votes on their own initiative. If so, PAP is false, and responsibility depends on how the action actually came about, not on whether alternatives were available.

Defenders of PAP have two main replies. The 'flicker of freedom' reply notes that Sam could still have shown the early sign that would have triggered the device. That residual alternative might ground his responsibility. Fischer responds that such a flicker is too thin, an involuntary twitch or neural pattern, to be the kind of control responsibility needs.

The dilemma defence (Kane, Widerker) is stronger. Either Sam's early sign reliably determines his later decision, or it does not. If it does, the case assumes something like determinism, which begs the question against incompatibilists who accept PAP. If it does not, Sam could have shown the 'Green' sign and still decided otherwise before the device could act, so he had alternatives after all. Refined cases, such as Mele and Robb's, in which the device's process runs alongside Sam's own without being triggered by a prior sign, try to escape the dilemma. Whether they succeed remains disputed.

If the Frankfurt intuition survives, it supports compatibilist accounts that focus on the actual sequence. An example is Fischer and Ravizza's guidance control, under which Sam acted from his own reasons-responsive mechanism.
