On balance, Sam is responsible, and the case makes PAP doubtful. But because of the dilemma defence, its force against incompatibilism is weaker than Frankfurt claimed.

questions.q: 'If determinism is true, no one is ever morally responsible for anything.' Discuss.
markScheme: Defines determinism and moral responsibility (e.g. basic-desert responsibility)
Presents the consequence argument (van Inwagen) and its transfer principle
Presents source incompatibilism / Basic Argument (Galen Strawson) or manipulation arguments (Pereboom's four-case)
Classical compatibilist reply (Hobbes, Hume): freedom as absence of constraint
Objection to classical compatibilism: conditional analysis of 'could have done otherwise'
Frankfurt cases and actual-sequence compatibilism
Hierarchical (Frankfurt 1971) or reasons-responsive (Fischer and Ravizza) accounts
P. F. Strawson's reactive attitudes approach
Considers the luck objection to libertarian alternatives (indeterminism may not help)
Considers hard incompatibilism and its practical implications (Pereboom)
Distinguishes forward-looking from backward-looking responsibility
Reaches a well-argued conclusion
questions.modelAnswer:
Determinism holds that the past and the laws of nature fix a single future. The claim is that, if this is true, no one deserves praise or blame for anything.

The strongest case for it is van Inwagen's consequence argument. If determinism is true, our acts follow from the laws and events before we were born. We have no power over the laws or the remote past, and powerlessness transfers through entailment. So we have no power over our acts. Source incompatibilists add that responsibility requires being the ultimate origin of one's actions. Pereboom's four-case argument presses this. An agent manipulated by neuroscientists into reasoning a certain way is not responsible. His case cannot be relevantly distinguished from that of an ordinary agent whose character comes from genes and upbringing in a deterministic world.

Compatibilists reply in several ways. Hobbes and Hume locate freedom in acting according to one's will without external constraint. That fits much ordinary practice, since we excuse coercion, not causation. But their conditional analysis of 'could have done otherwise' (I would have, had I chosen) fails if my choosing was itself impossible. Frankfurt cases suggest that alternative possibilities are not needed for responsibility. Actual-sequence accounts follow: Frankfurt's hierarchy of desires, and Fischer and Ravizza's reasons-responsive mechanisms that the agent has taken as their own. These give principled reasons to distinguish the manipulated agent from the ordinary one, by appeal to history and ownership. P. F. Strawson goes further. Our practices of resentment and gratitude are part of human life and need no metaphysical justification that determinism could remove.

Incompatibilists must also explain how indeterminism would help. If a choice is undetermined, the luck objection says its outcome looks like chance, not control. This leads Pereboom to hard incompatibilism: basic-desert responsibility is impossible either way. Forward-looking practices such as moral education, protection and reconciliation remain.

The proposition is plausible only for a demanding notion of ultimate, basic-desert responsibility. For the reasons-responsive responsibility our practices actually track, compatibilism offers a convincing account. Determinism threatens a particular philosophical ideal of responsibility rather than responsibility as such.

questions.q: Nurse Okoye works in an overstretched hospital. Five patients will die within days without organ transplants. A healthy visitor, Tom, is a perfect tissue match for all five. Okoye could secretly sedate Tom and remove his organs, saving five lives at the cost of one, with almost no chance of discovery. How would act utilitarianism, Kantian ethics and virtue ethics assess this action? Which gives the most convincing verdict?
markScheme: Act utilitarianism: identifies the apparent verdict that killing Tom maximises utility (five lives versus one)
Utilitarian replies: secrecy is unlikely in reality; indirect effects (trust in hospitals); rule utilitarianism forbids
Notes that these replies are contingent, so the case exposes the separateness of persons objection
Kantian: Formula of Humanity forbids using Tom merely as a means; no consent
Kantian: Universal Law test applied to the maxim
Virtue ethics: a just, compassionate, honest practitioner would not do this; it reflects vicious character and betrays professional role
Virtue ethics: discusses action-guidance and whether it simply follows intuition
Mentions doctrine of double effect or doing vs allowing as relevant deontological resources
Compares the three theories' verdicts and reasoning
Reaches a justified conclusion
questions.modelAnswer:
For act utilitarianism, the right act is the one that maximises overall well-being. On the stipulated facts, killing Tom saves five lives and costs one, with no risk of discovery. The theory seems to require the operation. Utilitarians often reply that in reality secrecy is improbable, and that the discovery of such practices would destroy trust in hospitals, so the expected consequences are bad. These replies depend on contingent facts. The case can be stipulated to remove them, leaving the verdict that Tom should be killed. That shows the theory permits sacrificing individuals whenever totals favour it. Rawls's objection is that it ignores the separateness of persons. Rule utilitarianism can forbid such killing, but it faces the collapse objection.

Kantian ethics clearly forbids the act. Sedating and dismantling Tom treats him merely as a means: he has not consented and could not rationally consent to being used up for others' benefit. The Formula of Universal Law points the same way. A rational agent could not will a maxim of killing anyone whose organs could save more lives, since it would make every person's life subject to such calculation. Deontologists can add the distinction between doing and allowing. Okoye would be killing Tom, whereas the five die from their illnesses.

Virtue ethics asks what a virtuous nurse would characteristically do (Hursthouse). Someone just, honest and caring, who respects the trust patients and visitors place in her role, would not secretly kill an innocent person. Such an act would display ruthlessness and a corrupted practical wisdom. Critics say virtue ethics only echoes our intuitions here. But its focus on character and roles explains why the act is abhorrent and not merely suboptimal.

The Kantian verdict is the most convincing because it explains the wrong directly. Tom is wronged, not merely harmed. Virtue ethics reaches the same verdict and adds the relevance of professional character. Act utilitarianism's verdict counts heavily against it.

questions.q: 'Virtue ethics cannot tell us what to do.' Discuss.
markScheme: Explains Aristotelian virtue ethics: eudaimonia, virtues as stable dispositions, the doctrine of the mean
Explains the role of phronesis (practical wisdom) in applying virtues to particulars
States the action-guidance objection clearly
Hursthouse's criterion of right action and v-rules (honesty, kindness, etc.)
Considers the objection that v-rules conflict and give no ranking
Compares with conflicts in Ross's deontology or the indeterminacy of utilitarian calculation
Discusses moral exemplars and moral education as forms of guidance
Discusses the circularity worry (virtuous agent defined by right action and vice versa)
Considers the situationist challenge (Doris, Harman) to stable traits
Considers whether demanding codified decision procedures is itself a mistake (Aristotle: precision appropriate to the subject matter)
Reaches a balanced conclusion
questions.modelAnswer:
Aristotle's virtue ethics locates morality in character. Virtues such as courage, justice and generosity are stable dispositions to feel and act well, each a mean between excess and deficiency. Together with practical wisdom (phronesis), they make up a flourishing life (eudaimonia). The objection is that 'be virtuous' gives no answer when I face a hard decision, such as whether to tell a dying friend an upsetting truth. Utilitarianism and Kantianism, by contrast, seem to supply decision procedures.

Hursthouse replies that virtue ethics does specify right action: an act is right if it is what a virtuous agent would characteristically do in the circumstances. It also supplies many 'v-rules'. Every virtue term yields a prescription, such as 'do what is honest' or 'do what is kind', and every vice term yields a prohibition, such as 'do not do what is cruel'. These are as action-guiding as Ross's prima facie duties.

The objection then returns in a narrower form. Honesty and kindness can conflict in the dying-friend case, and virtue ethics offers no rule for ranking them. It relies on the judgement of the practically wise person. But Ross's deontology faces the same problem of conflicting duties, and utilitarian 'guidance' often depends on predictions no one can make. If the objection works, it threatens every plausible theory, not only virtue ethics.

A related worry is circularity. If right action is defined by what the virtuous agent does, and the virtuous agent is defined by right action, nothing has been explained. Hursthouse breaks the circle by defining virtues as traits a human being needs in order to flourish. Situationists such as Doris and Harman ask whether robust traits exist at all, which would leave the virtuous-agent standard empty. Defenders reply that virtue is rare and is an ideal to aspire to.

Aristotle noted that ethics allows only the precision its subject matter permits. Demanding an algorithm may misunderstand moral life. Moral exemplars and moral education also guide action in ways rules cannot.

The objection is therefore overstated. Virtue ethics guides action, but through trained judgement rather than mechanical procedures.

questions.q: Two students disagree. Leila says: 'When I call factory farming wrong, I am stating a fact, just as I would be if I said the Earth orbits the Sun.' Ben replies: 'No, you're expressing your disapproval, and trying to get me to share it. There's no moral fact to be right about.' Assess the strongest considerations on each side and reach a view.
markScheme: Identifies Leila as a cognitivist / realist and Ben as an expressivist / emotivist (Ayer, Stevenson)
Ben: motivational internalism plus the Humean theory of motivation supports non-cognitivism
Ben: metaphysical and epistemological economy; queerness (Mackie) as supporting anti-realism
Ben: disagreement and its explanation
Leila: moral discourse has realist surface features (truth, assertion, reasoning)
Leila: the Frege–Geach problem for Ben's view
Leila: moral progress and the possibility of error
Ben's possible reply: Blackburn's quasi-realism
Considers naturalist vs non-naturalist versions of Leila's realism and the open question argument
Reaches a reasoned judgement
questions.modelAnswer:
Leila is a cognitivist and moral realist: 'factory farming is wrong' expresses a belief that can be true or false, made true by moral fact. Ben is a non-cognitivist in the tradition of Ayer and Stevenson: the judgement expresses an attitude and tries to persuade others to share it.

Ben's view has strong motivations. Moral judgements seem connected to motivation. Someone who sincerely judges factory farming wrong is usually moved to avoid supporting it, which supports motivational internalism. If, with Hume, beliefs alone cannot motivate, moral judgements must be desire-like states, not beliefs. Ben's view is also metaphysically economical. It avoids what Mackie called 'queer' entities, facts that are somehow intrinsically action-guiding and known by a special faculty. And it explains persistent disagreement as a clash of attitudes.

Leila can point to the realist surface of moral discourse. We call moral claims true, reason from them, and treat ourselves and others as capable of moral error. The Frege–Geach problem is especially pressing for Ben. In 'if factory farming is wrong, then subsidising it is wrong', no disapproval of factory farming is expressed. Yet the sentence means the same as when asserted alone, and it licenses a valid modus ponens. Ben owes an account of how attitudes combine logically. Leila can also appeal to moral progress. The abolition of slavery looks like correcting a mistake, not merely changing attitudes.

Ben can adopt Blackburn's quasi-realism, explaining moral truth-talk and logic in terms of attitudes. Whether this succeeds, or ends up so close to realism that the difference disappears, is a live question. Leila must say what kind of fact she has in mind. Natural facts face Moore's open question argument, although realists of the Cornell school reply that moral facts are discovered a posteriori, like water = H₂O. Non-natural facts face Mackie's queerness worry.

On balance, the logical and phenomenological evidence favours Leila's cognitivism, and the open question argument is not decisive against naturalist realism. But Ben's challenge about motivation and metaphysics means realism must be developed carefully, not merely assumed.

questions.q: Evaluate Mackie's claim that 'there are no objective values'.
markScheme: States Mackie's error theory: moral claims purport to report objective, categorically prescriptive facts, but there are none
Distinguishes the conceptual claim (ordinary moral thought presupposes objectivity) from the ontological claim
Explains the argument from relativity and its best-explanation structure
Responds to relativity: disagreement in science; agreement on core principles; factual disagreements
Explains the argument from queerness: metaphysical (intrinsic prescriptivity) and epistemological (special faculty)
Responds to queerness: companions in guilt (epistemic norms, mathematics); naturalist realism (Cornell realists)
Discusses the supervenience aspect of queerness
Considers alternatives: non-cognitivism (deny error) and constructivism
Considers the practical consequences: moral fictionalism or continuing moral practice
Considers the Moorean reply: more certain that cruelty is wrong than of Mackie's premises
Uses examples effectively
Reaches a well-argued conclusion
questions.modelAnswer:
In Ethics: Inventing Right and Wrong (1977), Mackie makes two claims. The conceptual claim is that ordinary moral thought presupposes objective, categorically prescriptive values. Wrongness is supposed to give reasons to anyone, whatever their desires. The ontological claim is that no such values exist. So moral judgements are systematically false. This is error theory, not non-cognitivism.

The argument from relativity is an inference to the best explanation. Moral codes vary greatly, and this is better explained by people's participation in different ways of life than by some people perceiving objective values more accurately. Realists can reply that scientific disagreement has never shown there are no scientific facts. Moral variation is often greater in application than in principle, since most cultures condemn gratuitous cruelty. Much moral disagreement also comes from differing factual beliefs. The argument raises a question for realism but does not settle it.

The argument from queerness is stronger. Metaphysically, objective values would have to be built so that knowing them gives a reason to act regardless of desire, which is unlike anything else in the world. Epistemologically, we would need a special faculty of moral intuition to detect them. Mackie also asks how moral properties relate to the natural features they supervene on.

Realists have answers. Naturalists such as the Cornell realists identify moral properties with complex natural properties discovered a posteriori, which removes the queerness at the risk of losing categorical authority. The 'companions in guilt' reply notes that epistemic norms are also categorical and objective. A good reason to believe something is a reason for anyone, so if Mackie's argument removes moral values, it threatens epistemic ones as well, including the norms his own argument relies on. And a Moorean may insist we are more certain that torturing for fun is wrong than we are of any premise about queerness.

Expressivists and constructivists offer further alternatives, denying either the error or the need for independent facts.

Mackie identifies real difficulties for non-naturalist realism, but the companions-in-guilt reply in particular shows that 'there are no objective values' has not been established.

questions.q: Clara, a junior doctor, lies to an anxious patient, telling him his biopsy results are 'not back yet' to spare him a night of worry before the consultant explains the diagnosis in the morning. Her motive is compassion. Using both the Formula of Universal Law and the Formula of Humanity, assess whether Kant's ethics condemns Clara's lie, and evaluate whether Kant's verdict is plausible.
markScheme: Formulates Clara's maxim precisely; notes that the test depends on how the maxim is described
Universal Law: if everyone lied whenever it spared distress, assurances would lose credibility (contradiction in conception)
Considers whether a narrowly described maxim can be universalised, and the problem of maxim description
Humanity: the lie bypasses the patient's rational agency, so he is used merely as a means, even benevolently
Notes that respect for autonomy has a special place in medical ethics and that this supports Kant
Moral worth: compassionate motive alone does not give moral worth (acting from duty)
Refers to 'On a Supposed Right to Lie' (1797) and Kant's rigorism about lying
Evaluates: Kant correctly identifies paternalism; but the verdict may seem too rigid where harm is small
Considers Kantian resources: imperfect duty of beneficence, alternatives (declining to answer)
Reaches a reasoned conclusion
questions.modelAnswer:
Clara's maxim might be: 'When telling the truth would cause a patient distress, I will tell him a falsehood to spare him.'

Under the Formula of Universal Law, we imagine everyone, or every doctor, acting on this maxim. Patients would then know that reassurances like 'results not back yet' might be comforting lies, and such statements would lose their credibility. Clara's lie works only because doctors' statements are generally trusted, so the maxim cannot be universalised without undermining itself. That is a contradiction in conception, which grounds a perfect duty not to lie. A narrowly tailored maxim ('lie only for one night, only about biopsy timing') might pass, which shows the problem of maxim description. Kantians usually require the maxim to state the agent's real principle: lying to spare distress.

The Formula of Humanity gives a clearer verdict. Lying to someone controls his beliefs without his rational consent. The patient loses the chance to decide how to spend the night, whether preparing, calling family or asking questions. Even a kindly lie treats him merely as a means to his own comfort, which is paternalism. Clara's compassionate motive does not change this. For Kant, moral worth comes from acting from duty, and inclinations, however attractive, do not make an act right. Since Kant held in 'On a Supposed Right to Lie' (1797) that even lying to a murderer at the door is wrong, Clara's lie is clearly condemned.

Is this plausible? In medical ethics the verdict has real force. Respect for patient autonomy is central, and the Kantian analysis explains why benevolent deception is objectionable. Kant also leaves Clara honest options. She could say she cannot discuss the results tonight, which avoids both lying and distress, while the imperfect duty of beneficence still asks her to show care. Where a lie causes trivial deception and prevents real suffering, the absolute prohibition can seem rigid, and many readers find Kant's own murderer case counterintuitive.

On balance Kant rightly condemns Clara's lie. The availability of honest alternatives makes the verdict more acceptable here than in the murderer case.

questions.q: 'Kant's answer to Hume on causation succeeds only at the price of making the world we know a mere appearance.' Discuss.
markScheme: Sets out Hume's position: no impression of necessary connection; causation as constant conjunction plus habit; the problem of induction
Explains that Kant credits Hume with waking him from 'dogmatic slumber' (Prolegomena)
Explains Kant's question about synthetic a priori judgements and the Copernican revolution
Explains the categories and the Transcendental Deduction: concepts necessary for unified experience
Explains the Second Analogy: objective succession requires a rule, so every event has a cause
Assesses whether Kant answers Hume's specific challenge (the principle versus particular causal laws; induction)
Explains transcendental idealism: phenomena versus things in themselves
Discusses the 'price': whether knowledge restricted to appearances is a real cost (two-worlds vs two-aspects readings)
Considers objections: the thing in itself and applying causality to it (Jacobi); whether idealism is required (e.g. Strawson's The Bounds of Sense)
Considers whether the idealism is the source of the a priori necessity, so the price is unavoidable
Uses Kant's texts accurately
Reaches a well-argued conclusion
questions.modelAnswer:
Hume argued that we perceive only constant conjunction, never necessary connection. The idea of necessity comes from habit, and inferences beyond experience cannot be justified without circularity. Kant, woken from his 'dogmatic slumber' (Prolegomena, 1783), agreed necessity cannot come from experience but denied it is mere habit.

Kant's strategy is the Copernican turn. Objects must conform to the conditions of our cognition. Space and time are forms of intuition, and the categories, including cause and effect, are pure concepts of the understanding. The Transcendental Deduction argues that without the categories our representations could not be unified in one self-conscious experience of objects. The Second Analogy applies this to causality. We tell an objective succession (a ship moving downstream) from a subjective one (scanning a house) only by representing the order as fixed by a rule. So every event follows something according to a rule, and the causal principle is a condition of experience itself, known synthetically a priori.

The reply is limited. It establishes that every event has a cause, but not particular causal laws, so Hume's problem of induction about them largely remains. Kant's answer also has a cost. The principle holds necessarily only because objects of experience are partly constituted by our cognition. It therefore applies only to appearances, and things as they are in themselves remain unknowable. Jacobi objected that Kant needs things in themselves to affect us causally while denying causality applies beyond experience.

How great the cost is depends on interpretation. On a two-worlds reading, the world we know becomes a realm of representations, uncomfortably close to Berkeley. On Allison's two-aspect reading, they are the same objects considered in two ways, and the restriction is epistemic modesty. P. F. Strawson (The Bounds of Sense, 1966) tried to separate the Deduction's analytical core from the idealism.

The idealism therefore seems to be what grounds the necessity, so the price is real. On the two-aspect reading, though, it is a limit on what we can know, not a reduction of the known world to mere appearance.
